title: The Xtabai of Temptress Creek
summary: A beautiful woman lures men into the jungle on moonlit nights, but those who follow the Xtabai discover too late that her beauty is a veil over ancient hunger, and the jungle keeps what she claims.
full_text:
Along the banks of the Temptress Creek, which winds through the broadleaf forest between the Stann Creek and Toledo districts, the old people tell of a woman who is not a woman. They call her Xtabai, and they say she has lived in these woods since before the Maya built their first temple.

She appears on nights when the moon is full and the air is thick with the scent of wild orchids. She stands at the edge of the tree line where the forest meets the riverbank, and she is beautiful in a way that makes the mind go quiet. Her hair is long and black and moves as though underwater. Her skin glows faintly, as though lit by a fire inside her. She wears a white dress that touches the ground.

Men who see her feel a pull that is not desire exactly, though it uses desire as its door. It is more like homesickness, a longing for something they cannot name. They leave their hammocks, their fires, their sleeping families, and they walk toward her. She never approaches them. She simply stands, and they come.

An old fisherman named Don Aurelio told the story of his brother, Marcos, who was claimed by the Xtabai thirty years ago. 'Marcos was a strong man,' Don Aurelio said, rolling a cigarette with hands that shook. 'He laughed at everything. He was not afraid of jaguars or spirits or anything in this world. One night he heard a woman singing by the creek. He said he was going to see who it was. I told him, leave it alone. But Marcos was Marcos.'

Marcos walked to the riverbank in his undershirt, carrying nothing. Don Aurelio watched from the doorway of their hut. In the moonlight, he could see the figure of a woman standing among the mahogany trees. Marcos called out to her. She turned, and even from that distance Don Aurelio felt something cold pass through his chest.

Marcos walked into the tree line and did not come back. They searched for three days. They found his machete near the riverbank, standing upright in the mud as though someone had placed it there as a marker. But of Marcos, nothing.

Don Aurelio said the Xtabai does not kill in the way a jaguar kills. She takes the whole person, body and shadow, and they become part of the forest. Sometimes, on very quiet nights, you can hear men calling from deep in the jungle. Not in pain. In wonder. As though they have found something they did not know they were looking for and cannot find their way back to the ordinary world.

The old people say the only protection against the Xtabai is to never walk toward beauty that you have not been invited to meet. If a woman stands at the tree line who should not be there, you turn your back and you walk away, and you do not look over your shoulder, and you do not wonder what she wanted. Because the wondering is how she takes you.
themes: the jungle as a living force
moral: Not every beautiful thing that calls to you has your best interests at heart. Some invitations are traps dressed in moonlight.

title: The Xan of Mountain Passes
summary: A shepherd encounters a Xan, a restless mountain ghost, and learns why the dead sometimes refuse to leave the high places they loved in life.
full_text:
In the rugged passes of the Greater Caucasus, where mist clings to the stones like mourning cloth, there lived a shepherd named Orkhan. He tended his flocks along ridges so narrow that a single misstep would send a man tumbling into the valley below. The old women of his village warned him never to whistle after sunset, for whistling called the Xan.

The Xan were ghosts of those who had died in the mountains. Herders crushed by avalanches, warriors slain in border skirmishes, wanderers lost to the winter cold. Their spirits could not rest because the mountains had claimed them too suddenly, too violently. So they lingered, drifting through the passes like fog, their forms flickering between the living and the gone.

Orkhan had never believed. He was a practical man, more concerned with the weight of his cheese bundles than the weight of old superstitions. But one autumn evening, as he drove his flock down from the high meadow, the temperature dropped with unnatural speed. The goats bleated in panic and huddled together. A figure appeared on the trail ahead, standing where no man could stand on such a narrow ledge.

It wore the clothes of a herder from three generations past. Its face was not cruel, but it carried an expression of profound confusion, as though it had been walking for a very long time and could not remember why. The Xan looked at Orkhan with hollow eyes and spoke, though its voice sounded like wind through a crevice: 'Do you know the way down? I have forgotten the way down.'

Orkhan's first instinct was to run, but something in the ghost's sorrow held him. He thought of his own grandfather, who had vanished in a blizzard twenty years ago and whose body was never found. Perhaps this was one of the lost ones, trapped between the peak and the valley, between death and memory.

He took off his woolen scarf and held it out. The Xan reached for it, and where its fingers touched the fabric, the wool grew ice-cold but did not tear. Orkhan tied one end to a rock and laid the scarf along the path, a thread of warmth marking the way downward. He walked ahead, and the Xan followed, step by careful step, its bare feet leaving no prints in the dust.

When they reached the tree line, where the mountain gives way to forest and the living world begins again, the Xan paused. The confusion had left its face, replaced by something like gratitude. It touched Orkhan's shoulder, and the cold was so deep it burned, but only for a moment. Then the ghost walked into the trees and did not return.

Orkhan retrieved his scarf the next morning. It was whole but stiff with frost that would never melt. He kept it hanging above his hearth for the rest of his days, a reminder that the mountains hold their dead close, and that the dead sometimes need a gentle hand to guide them home.

From that day, he never mocked the old women's warnings. He taught his own children to leave a scarf or a ribbon tied to a stone at the mountain's edge, a small offering for those who wandered the passes. And when the autumn winds blew cold and strange through the village, the people would say that the Xan were walking again, searching for the way down.
moral: The dead deserve compassion, not fear. A small act of kindness can release a sorrow that has lasted generations.

title: Xnifs, the Goblin of the Megaliths
summary: A small, hairy goblin who haunts the ancient megalithic temples of Malta, sometimes helpful and sometimes malicious.
full_text:
Malta is a land of ancient stone. The temples of the Neolithic people stand silent on the hills, older than the pyramids, older than Stonehenge. And among these stones, the Maltese say, lives the Xnifs. A small, hairy creature, no bigger than a cat, with long arms and a face like a wrinkled old man. He darts between the megaliths when no one is looking, leaving footprints in the dust that vanish by morning.

The Xnifs is a remnant of the old world, a spirit that was here before the Phoenicians, before the Romans, before the Knights of St. John. He does not speak, but he understands the speech of men. He is drawn to the temples, especially the great complex at Ġgantija on Gozo, where the stones are so massive that legend says a giantess carried them. The Xnifs knows the secrets of these places. He knows where the hidden chambers are, where the old offerings were buried.

Sometimes the Xnifs helps. A shepherd who loses a goat near the Ħaġar Qim temple may find the animal waiting for him at the temple gate, bleating softly. A farmer whose well has run dry may hear a tapping sound in the night that leads him to a new spring. But the Xnifs also plays tricks. He hides tools. He tangles fishing nets. He whispers in the dark, making sleepers restless.

The only way to gain the Xnifs's favor is to leave a small offering of bread and olive oil at the temple entrance. The old women of Malta still do this, especially before the harvest. They say the Xnifs, though mischievous, has a good heart. He has been watching over the stones for five thousand years. He will be here long after we are gone.
moral: Honour the ancient ones who came before, for they still walk among the stones.
